description: We fly a lander onto the real surface of Jezero Crater on Mars, using the actual 1-metre HiRISE terrain data Perseverance's team used. A browser game, React + Three.js. You fire the thrusters, dust kicks up, and the game scores your touchdown.
summary: I got annoyed at Mars maps. Everyone makes a map. So I made a game where you actually land on Mars. You fly a lander down onto Jezero Crater, on the real terrain data. Same 1-metre HiRISE heightmap Perseverance's team used to pick their landing spot. The camera dives in from orbit, you fire the thrusters, dust kicks up, and you either stick the landing or you don't. My demo flight landed SAFE, 85/100, 30 m from the target. The scoring uses the real elevations and slopes from the data, not a heightmap I made up.
details:
What it is: a web game, React + Three.js. No backend, no login. Open the link and fly. The flight: you start 950 m up, 650 m east of the target, already drifting toward it. Mars gravity is 3.71 m/s2, you've got a main thruster and side thrusters, and not much fuel. Land inside the gold ring at Octavia E. Butler Landing (18.44N, 77.45E). How it scores you: how fast you're falling (safe is under 3.5 m/s), how fast you're sliding sideways (under 2.5 m/s), the actual slope where you touch down (under 12 degrees), how far from the target (under 150 m), and fuel left. All of it adds up to a score out of 100. The terrain: a 6 x 6 km patch of Jezero from the USGS Mars 2020 HiRISE DTM mosaic, 1 m per point, squeezed down to a 256 x 256 heightmap. The texture is the matching HiRISE photo of the surface. The photo strip doesn't cover the eastern 16.1% of the patch, so those pixels are a hillshade made from the same height data, matched to blend in. The 3D mesh is stretched 2.5x taller so you can actually see the terrain. The physics and scoring always use the true heights. How to play: Space or up arrow for the main thruster, W to push forward, left and right arrows to steer, down arrow to pull back, R to retry. Touch buttons on mobile. A full landing takes about 30 seconds.

Use of AI: Muse (Meta) + Claude wrote the game code, the terrain-conversion script, and this project text from my design brief, with me directing it. No AI-made images: the terrain texture is the real HiRISE photo (eastern 16.1% is a hillshade fill from the same data, since the photo strip doesn't cover it); the lander is built from plain 3D shapes. No AI played the game or made the demo video.
